claim: The time course of transmitter release at inhibitory basket cell-Purkinje cell synapses is independent of extracellular Ca2+ concentration ([Ca2+]o).
source: Here, we examine the time course of release at inhibitory basket cell-Purkinje cell synapses and show that it is independent of [Ca2+]o.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Tight coupling between Ca2+ channels and release sensors provides a mechanistic explanation for the [Ca2+]o independence of the time course of release.
source: Thus, tight channel-sensor coupling provides a mechanistic explanation for the apparent [Ca2+]o independence of the time course of release.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by modeling and experimental data with Ca2+ chelators.

claim: The mean distance between Ca2+ channels and release sensors at basket cell-Purkinje cell synapses is 10–20 nm.
source: Experiments with exogenous Ca2+ chelators reveal that channel-sensor coupling at basket cell-Purkinje cell synapses is very tight, with a mean distance of 10–20 nm.
evidence: This distance estimate is derived from experiments using BAPTA and EGTA chelators and fitting with diffusion models.

claim: The time course of release at the neuromuscular junction is independent of extracellular Ca2+ concentration.
source: In contrast to this expectation, the time course of release (TCR) at the neuromuscular junction is independent of the extracellular Ca2+ concentration ([Ca2+]o) (Datyner and Gage, 1980; Van der Kloot, 1988; Parnas et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The apparent [Ca2+]o independence of the time course of release is less well established at central synapses.
source: However, the apparent [Ca2+]o independence of the TCR is less well established at central synapses (Sargent et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sargent et al., 2005.

claim: Tight coupling between presynaptic Ca2+ channels and release sensors has been observed in several central synapses.
source: Recent results suggested that in several central synapses presynaptic Ca2+ channels and release sensors are tightly coupled (Bucurenciu et al., 2008; Eggermann et al., 2012; Scimemi and Diamond, 2012; Schmidt et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Synaptic latency at basket cell-Purkinje cell synapses is 1.20 ± 0.03 ms at ~22°C.
source: Synaptic latency was 1.20 ± 0.03 ms at ∼22°C (24 pairs) and 0.47 ± 0.02 ms at ∼34°C (5 pairs; Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This measurement is directly reported from experimental data and shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Synaptic latency at basket cell-Purkinje cell synapses is 0.47 ± 0.02 ms at ~34°C.
source: Synaptic latency was 1.20 ± 0.03 ms at ∼22°C (24 pairs) and 0.47 ± 0.02 ms at ∼34°C (5 pairs; Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This measurement is directly reported from experimental data and shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Transmitter release at basket cell-Purkinje cell synapses is entirely blocked by the P/Q-type Ca2+ channel blocker ω-agatoxin IVa (1 µM).
source: Synaptic transmission was entirely blocked by bath application of the selective P/Q-type Ca2+ channel blocker ω-agatoxin IVa (1 µM), whereas the N-type Ca2+ channel blocker ω-conotoxin GVIa (1 µM) had no detectable effect (Figure 1E–H).
evidence: This finding is directly reported from experimental data shown in Figure 1E-H.

claim: The N-type Ca2+ channel blocker ω-conotoxin GVIa (1 µM) has no detectable effect on transmitter release at basket cell-Purkinje cell synapses.
source: Synaptic transmission was entirely blocked by bath application of the selective P/Q-type Ca2+ channel blocker ω-agatoxin IVa (1 µM), whereas the N-type Ca2+ channel blocker ω-conotoxin GVIa (1 µM) had no detectable effect (Figure 1E–H).
evidence: This finding is directly reported from experimental data shown in Figure 1E-H.

claim: Transmitter release at basket cell-Purkinje cell synapses is selectively mediated by P/Q-type Ca2+ channels.
source: Thus, transmitter release at this synapse is selectively mediated by P/Q-type Ca2+ channels.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the differential effects of ω-agatoxin IVa and ω-conotoxin GVIa shown in Figure 1.

claim: The dependence of evoked IPSC peak amplitude on [Ca2+]o at basket cell-Purkinje cell synapses has a high power coefficient (n = 3.02 in the low-concentration limit).
source: Analysis of the dependence of evoked IPSC peak amplitude on [Ca2+]o revealed that the amount of transmitter release was steeply [Ca2+]o-dependent, with a high power coefficient (n = 3.02 in the low-concentration limit; Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This power coefficient is calculated from experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Release at basket cell-Purkinje cell synapses is highly cooperative.
source: Thus, release at the BC–PC synapse was highly cooperative (Dodge and Rahamimoff, 1967).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the high power coefficient and is supported by citation to Dodge and Rahamimoff, 1967.

claim: When [Ca2+]o was changed in the range from 0.7–4 mM, peak release rate changed by a factor of 34.4.
source: When [Ca2+]o was changed in the range from 0.7–4 mM, peak release rate changed by a factor of 34.4.
evidence: This quantitative result is directly reported from experimental measurements.

claim: The half-duration of the time course of release is minimally affected by changes in [Ca2+]o from 0.7-4 mM (0.49 ± 0.05 ms at 0.7 mM; 0.43 ± 0.05 ms at 1 mM; 0.47 ± 0.01 ms at 2 mM; 0.47 ± 0.02 ms at 4 mM; p = 0.56).
source: In contrast, the half-duration of the TCR was only minimally affected (0.49 ± 0.05 ms at 0.7 mM; 0.43 ± 0.05 ms at 1 mM; 0.47 ± 0.01 ms at 2 mM; 0.47 ± 0.02 ms at 4 mM; 5–11 pairs; p = 0.56; Figure 2D,E).
evidence: These measurements are directly reported from experimental data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: The decay time constant of the time course of release is similar across different [Ca2+]o conditions (p = 0.38).
source: Furthermore, the decay time constant of the TCR was similar in the different conditions (p = 0.38; Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This statistical result is directly reported from experimental data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: At ~12°C, changes in [Ca2+]o have no detectable effects on the half-duration of the time course of release (2.84 ± 0.42 ms at 1 mM, 2.97 ± 0.24 ms at 2 mM, and 2.79 ± 0.25 ms at 4 mM [Ca2+]o; p = 0.93).
source: At ∼12°C, changes in [Ca2+]o had no detectable effects on the half-duration of the TCR (2.84 ± 0.42 ms at 1 mM, 2.97 ± 0.24 ms at 2 mM, and 2.79 ± 0.25 ms at 4 mM [Ca2+]o; 5 pairs; p = 0.93) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: These measurements are directly reported from experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The time course of release is markedly dependent on peak release rate in both low and high peak release rate limits in computational models.
source: Computational analysis revealed that the TCR was markedly dependent on the PRR in both low and high PRR limit.
evidence: This finding is derived from computational modeling shown in Figure 3.

claim: In the low peak release rate limit, the half-duration of the time course of release decreases with peak release rate in a model with fixed coupling distance.
source: In the low PRR limit, the half-duration of the TCR decreased with PRR in a model with fixed coupling distance (Figure 3C).
evidence: This behavior is shown in computational modeling results in Figure 3C.

claim: Rate-limiting sensor kinetics are responsible for the dependence of time course of release on peak release rate in the low peak release rate limit.
source: This dependence was accentuated after slowing of release sensor rates (Figure 3D, top), indicating that rate-limiting sensor kinetics are responsible.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from computational modeling results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In the high peak release rate limit, the half-duration of the time course of release increases with peak release rate.
source: In the high PRR limit, the half-duration of the TCR increased with PRR (Figure 3C).
evidence: This behavior is shown in computational modeling results in Figure 3C.

claim: Saturation of endogenous buffers leads to broadening of the time course of release in small boutons at high peak release rates.
source: This behavior was particularly prominent in small boutons (Figure 3F, bottom), suggesting that saturation of the endogenous buffers leads to broadening of the TCR.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from computational modeling results shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The coupling distance plays a key role in determining the shape of the time course of release vs peak release rate relation in all conditions examined.
source: Thus, whereas several factors influence the shape of the TCR–PRR relation, the coupling distance plays a key role in all conditions examined.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from computational modeling results shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The fast Ca2+ chelator BAPTA markedly suppresses transmitter release at basket cell-Purkinje cell synapses.
source: Whereas the fast Ca2+ chelator ethylenedioxybis-(o-phenylenenitrilo)-N,N,N',N'-tetraacetic acid (BAPTA) markedly suppressed transmitter release (Figure 4A,B), the slow Ca2+ chelator ethyleneglycol-bis(2-aminoethylether)-N,N,N',N'-tetraacetic acid (EGTA) was much less effective (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This finding is directly reported from experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The slow Ca2+ chelator EGTA is much less effective than BAPTA at suppressing transmitter release at basket cell-Purkinje cell synapses.
source: Whereas the fast Ca2+ chelator ethylenedioxybis-(o-phenylenenitrilo)-N,N,N',N'-tetraacetic acid (BAPTA) markedly suppressed transmitter release (Figure 4A,B), the slow Ca2+ chelator ethyleneglycol-bis(2-aminoethylether)-N,N,N',N'-tetraacetic acid (EGTA) was much less effective (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This finding is directly reported from experimental data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: The half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) for the steady-state effect of BAPTA is 0.6 mM.
source: Analysis of concentration–effect data revealed that the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) for the steady-state effect was 0.6 mM for BAPTA (14 pairs total) and 16.0 mM for EGTA (11 pairs total; Figure 4E).
evidence: This IC50 value is calculated from experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) for the steady-state effect of EGTA is 16.0 mM.
source: Analysis of concentration–effect data revealed that the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) for the steady-state effect was 0.6 mM for BAPTA (14 pairs total) and 16.0 mM for EGTA (11 pairs total; Figure 4E).
evidence: This IC50 value is calculated from experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The IC50 value is ~27-fold higher for EGTA than for BAPTA.
source: Thus, the IC50 value was ∼27-fold higher for EGTA than for BAPTA.
evidence: This ratio is calculated from the IC50 values reported for BAPTA and EGTA.

claim: For the single-channel model, the coupling distance was estimated as 11.4 nm.
source: For the single-channel model, the coupling distance was estimated as 11.4 nm.
evidence: This estimate is derived from fitting experimental data with a model of Ca2+ diffusion and buffering.

claim: For the half-normal distribution model, the standard deviation of coupling distance was 10.5 nm (expectation value 13.9 nm; skewness 1.0).
source: For the half-normal distribution, the standard deviation was 10.5 nm (expectation value 13.9 nm; skewness 1.0).
evidence: This estimate is derived from fitting experimental data with a model of Ca2+ diffusion and buffering.

claim: For the skewed-normal distribution model, location, scale, and shape parameters were 13.7 nm, 8.6 nm, and −1.11, respectively (expectation value 10.1 nm; skewness 0.40).
source: For the skewed-normal distribution, location, scale, and shape parameter were 13.7 nm, 8.6 nm, and −1.11, respectively (expectation value 10.1 nm; skewness 0.40).
evidence: This estimate is derived from fitting experimental data with a model of Ca2+ diffusion and buffering.

claim: Statistical errors in coupling distance estimates are minimal (1.2 nm).
source: Statistical errors, as assessed by bootstrap analysis, were minimal (1.2 nm; Figure 4G).
evidence: This error estimate is derived from bootstrap analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Systematic errors in coupling distance estimates are small, as indicated by robustness against variations in resting Ca2+ concentration and endogenous buffer product.
source: Furthermore, systematic errors were small, as indicated by the robustness of the estimate against variations in resting Ca2+ concentration and endogenous buffer product (Figure 4H).
evidence: This assessment is based on sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The coupling between Ca2+ channels and release sensors at cerebellar basket cell-Purkinje cell synapses is tight.
source: These results reveal that the coupling between Ca2+ channels and release sensors at the cerebellar BC–PC synapse is tight.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the coupling distance estimates of 10-20 nm.

claim: While the amount of release is highly [Ca2+]o-dependent with a power coefficient of ~3, the time course of release is largely [Ca2+]o-independent at basket cell-Purkinje cell synapses.
source: Our results demonstrate that while the amount of release is highly [Ca2+]o-dependent with a power coefficient of ∼3, the TCR is largely [Ca2+]o-independent.
evidence: This summary statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The [Ca2+]o independence of the time course of release is a general phenomenon characteristic for synaptic transmission in both peripheral and central nervous system.
source: Thus, our results demonstrate that the [Ca2+]o independence of the TCR is a general phenomenon characteristic for synaptic transmission in both peripheral and central nervous system.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from comparing results at BC-PC synapses with previous findings at the neuromuscular junction.

claim: Tight coupling is primarily used at synapses designed for fast, reliable transmission, whereas loose coupling is utilized at synapses specialized on presynaptic plasticity.
source: It has been suggested that tight coupling is primarily used at synapses designed for fast, reliable transmission, whereas loose coupling is utilized at synapses specialized on presynaptic plasticity (Bucurenciu et al., 2008; Eggermann et al., 2012; Nadkarni et al., 2012; Vyleta and Jonas, 2014).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: GABAergic basket cell-Purkinje cell synapses show fast transmitter release following single action potentials and reliable transmission during trains of spikes.
source: The present results are fully consistent with this hypothesis, since GABAergic BC–PC synapses show fast transmitter release following single action potentials and reliable transmission during trains of spikes (Caillard et al., 2000; Sakaba, 2008; Eggermann and Jonas, 2012).
evidence: This characterization is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The model predicts that slowing of sensor rates should markedly enhance the [Ca2+]o dependence of the time course of release in a microdomain, but not in a nanodomain coupling regime.
source: Specifically, our model predicts that slowing of sensor rates should markedly enhance the [Ca2+]o dependence of the TCR in a microdomain, but not in a nanodomain coupling regime.
evidence: This prediction is derived from computational modeling results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Lowering the temperature had large effects on the absolute value of the half-duration of the time course of release, but its [Ca2+]o independence was unchanged.
source: Whereas lowering the temperature had large effects on the absolute value of the half-duration of the TCR, its [Ca2+]o independence was unchanged.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tight source–sensor coupling is a key factor that ensures the [Ca2+]o independence of the time course of release.
source: These findings provide experimental evidence that tight source–sensor coupling is a key factor that ensures the [Ca2+]o independence of the TCR.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combination of modeling predictions and experimental temperature manipulation results.

claim: Nanodomain coupling conveys [Ca2+]o independence to the time course of release.
source: Our results suggest another functional benefit: conveying [Ca2+]o independence to the TCR.
evidence: This functional benefit is inferred from the experimental and modeling results presented in the study.

claim: Feedforward inhibition mediated by basket cells sets the temporal window of signal integration in Purkinje cells.
source: Maintenance of speed and temporal precision at the GABAergic BC–PC synapse is of critical importance for the operation of the cerebellum, since feedforward inhibition mediated by BCs sets the temporal window of signal integration in PCs (Mittmann et al., 2005; Bao et al., 2010).
evidence: This functional role is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Extracellular Ca2+ concentration has been shown to fluctuate during repetitive activity, high-frequency network oscillations, and in pathophysiological conditions.
source: However, [Ca2+]o has been shown to fluctuate during repetitive activity, high-frequency network oscillations, and in pathophysiological conditions (Heinemann et al., 1977; Borst and Sakmann, 1999; Rusakov and Fine, 2003).
evidence: This phenomenon is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ca2+ inflow is changed by neuromodulators, which often act via inhibition of presynaptic Ca2+ channels.
source: Furthermore, Ca2+ inflow will be changed by neuromodulators, which often act via inhibition of presynaptic Ca2+ channels (Takahashi et al., 1998).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by a citation to Takahashi et al., 1998.

claim: Nanodomain coupling at basket cell-Purkinje cell synapses may ensure constant timing of fast feedforward inhibition under a variety of network conditions.
source: Thus, nanodomain coupling at BC–PC synapses may ensure constant timing of fast feedforward inhibition under a variety of network conditions.
evidence: This functional implication is inferred from the experimental findings and known physiological variations in Ca2+ concentration.

claim: Slices were cut from the cerebellum of 14- to 16-day-old C57/Bl6 wild-type mice of either sex.
source: Slices were cut from the cerebellum of 14- to 16-day-old C57/Bl6 wild-type mice of either sex.
evidence: This is a methodological detail directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Postsynaptic series resistance was 3.8 ± 0.1 MΩ (mean ± SEM; 92 cells).
source: IPSCs were recorded in the postsynaptic PC under whole-cell voltage-clamp conditions (series resistance 3.8 ± 0.1 MΩ; mean ± SEM; 92 cells; 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a methodological measurement directly reported in the Results section.

claim: At 2 mM [Ca2+]o, the quantal content, estimated as the integral under the time course of release, was 10.4 ± 1.8.
source: At 2 mM [Ca2+]o, the quantal content, estimated as the integral under the TCR, was 10.4 ± 1.8.
evidence: This measurement is directly reported in the Materials and methods section.

claim: In 4 mM [Ca2+]o, the half-duration of the time course of release was 0.51 ± 0.04 in the presence vs 0.47 ± 0.02 in the absence of TPMPA (p = 0.38).
source: In 4 mM [Ca2+]o (presumably maximizing the confounding effects of postsynaptic factors), the half-duration of the TCR was 0.51 ± 0.04 in the presence (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; 6 pairs) vs 0.47 ± 0.02 in the absence of TPMPA (Figure 2E; p = 0.38).
evidence: This measurement is reported in the Materials and methods section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: For BAPTA, the Ca2+ binding and unbinding rates were assumed as kon = 4 × 10^8 M^-1s^-1 and koff = 88 s^-1 (affinity 220 nM).
source: For BAPTA, the Ca2+ binding and unbinding rates were assumed as kon = 4 108 M-1s−1 and koff = 88 s−1 (affinity 220 nM).
evidence: These are model parameters stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: For EGTA, the Ca2+ binding and unbinding rates were assumed as kon = 1 × 10^7 M^-1s^-1 and koff = 0.7 s^-1 (affinity 70 nM).
source: For EGTA, the rates were taken as kon = 1 107 M-1s−1 and koff = 0.7 s−1 (affinity 70 nM).
evidence: These are model parameters stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The diffusion coefficients for Ca2+, EGTA, and BAPTA were assumed to be 220 µm^2 s^-1.
source: The diffusion coefficients for Ca2+, EGTA, and BAPTA were assumed to be 220 µm2 s−1 (Neher, 1998).
evidence: This model parameter is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by citation to Neher, 1998.

claim: The endogenous buffer product was set to 5500 s^-1.
source: The endogenous buffer product was set to 5500 s−1 and the resting Ca2+ concentration was assumed as 40 nM (Collin et al., 2005).
evidence: This model parameter is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The resting Ca2+ concentration was assumed as 40 nM.
source: The endogenous buffer product was set to 5500 s−1 and the resting Ca2+ concentration was assumed as 40 nM (Collin et al., 2005).
evidence: This model parameter is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by citation to Collin et al., 2005.

claim: The diameter of the release unit was assumed to be 1 µm, approximately corresponding to the radius of inhibitory boutons.
source: The diameter was assumed to be 1 µm, approximately corresponding to the radius of inhibitory boutons, unless specified differently.
evidence: This model parameter is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The single-channel conductance of P/Q-type Ca2+ channels was assumed as 2.2 pS.
source: The single-channel conductance was assumed as 2.2 pS (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: This model parameter is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by citation to Li et al., 2007.

claim: The maximal release rate in the model was 6008 s^-1.
source: The maximal release rate in the model was 6008 s−1 (Lou et al., 2005).
evidence: This model parameter is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by citation to Lou et al., 2005.

claim: Unitary IPSCs at basket cell-Purkinje cell synapses are initiated with short latency and high temporal precision.
source: Unitary IPSCs were initiated with short latency and high temporal precision.
evidence: This characterization is directly stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: The time course of release was determined by deconvolution of unitary and quantal IPSC waveforms.
source: We then computed the TCR by deconvolution of unitary and quantal IPSC waveforms (Diamond and Jahr, 1995; Neher and Sakaba, 2001; Sakaba, 2008; Figure 2D).
evidence: This methodological approach is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Ca2+ plays a key role in the control of transmitter release at chemical synapses.
source: Calcium plays a key role in the control of transmitter release at chemical synapses (Neher, 1998; Südhof, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Neher, 1998 and Südhof, 2013.

claim: Transmitter release is a Ca2+-dependent biochemical process.
source: As transmitter release is a Ca2+-dependent biochemical process, one would expect that both the extent and kinetics of release will depend on Ca2+ concentration.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction.

claim: Several potential explanations for the [Ca2+]o independence of the time course of release were proposed, including adaptation of transmitter release and additional voltage sensors that control the timing of release.
source: Several potential explanations were proposed, including adaptation of transmitter release (Hsu et al., 1996) and additional voltage sensors that control the timing of release (Parnas et al., 2000; See; Felmy et al., 2003).
evidence: These alternative explanations are mentioned with supporting citations.

claim: Tight coupling might be a factor contributing to the apparent [Ca2+]o independence of the time course of release.
source: Tight coupling might be another factor contributing to the apparent [Ca2+]o independence of the TCR (Yamada and Zucker, 1992).
evidence: This hypothesis is mentioned with a supporting citation to Yamada and Zucker, 1992.

claim: The possibility that tight coupling contributes to [Ca2+]o independence of the time course of release has not been directly examined prior to this study.
source: However, this possibility has not been directly examined.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Previous studies highlighted several functional advantages of nanodomain coupling, including efficacy, speed, temporal precision, and energy efficiency of synaptic transmission.
source: Previous studies highlighted several functional advantages of nanodomain coupling, including efficacy, speed, temporal precision, and energy efficiency of synaptic transmission (Bucurenciu et al., 2008; Eggermann et al., 2012).
evidence: This summary of previous findings is supported by citations.

claim: The rules that define the coupling configuration between Ca2+ channels and release sensors remain elusive.
source: Although several previous studies measured the coupling distance, the rules that define the coupling configuration remain elusive (Hefft and Jonas, 2005; Bucurenciu et al., 2008; Christie et al., 2011; Nadkarni et al., 2012; Scimemi and Diamond, 2012; Schmidt et al., 2013; Vyleta and Jonas, 2014).
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in understanding despite multiple previous studies.

claim: The [Ca2+]o dependence of the time course of release is substantially more prominent in loose than in tight coupling regimes in a variety of conditions including different Ca2+ sensor rates, different bouton diameters, various concentrations and affinity values of endogenous buffers, and uniform vs non-uniform coupling.
source: Our model reveals that the [Ca2+]o dependence is substantially more prominent in loose than in tight coupling regimes in a variety of conditions. These include different Ca2+ sensor rates, different bouton diameters, various concentrations and affinity values of endogenous buffers, and uniform vs non-uniform coupling.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from computational modeling results shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lowering the temperature is expected to slow sensor rates among other potential effects.
source: We tested this prediction by lowering the temperature, which, among other potential effects, is expected to slow sensor rates.
evidence: This is stated as a known effect of temperature on biochemical processes.

claim: Similar morphological properties were obtained in 29 other biocytin-labeled cerebellar basket cells.
source: Similar morphological properties were obtained in 29 other biocytin-labeled cerebellar BCs.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1A.

claim: The evoked IPSC shows only little rundown for more than 40 min with stable series resistance.
source: Note that evoked IPSC shows only little rundown for more than 40 min with stable series resistance.
evidence: This observation is noted in the caption of Figure 1B and shown in the figure.

claim: The Hill equation fit to the IPSC-[Ca2+]o data yielded a maximal value (a) of 3.73, a half-maximal effective concentration (EC50) of 3.09 mM, and an average Hill coefficient (n) of 2.39.
source: Data were fit with a Hill equation, yielding a maximal value (a) of 3.73, a half-maximal effective concentration (EC50) of 3.09 mM, and an average Hill coefficient (n) of 2.39.
evidence: These fit parameters are reported in the caption of Figure 2B.

claim: The peak amplitude of IPSC successes reaches a constant level below 1 mM [Ca2+]o, suggesting that the level of quantal IPSCs was reached.
source: The peak amplitude of the successes reaches a constant level below 1 mM [Ca2+]o, suggesting that the level of quantal IPSCs was reached.
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the caption of Figure 2C.

claim: Action potentials, evoked IPSCs, and quantal IPSCs are markedly slower at ~12°C than at ~22°C.
source: Note that the action potentials, evoked IPSCs, and quantal IPSCs are markedly slower than those obtained at ∼22°C (compare with Figure 2A,C).
evidence: This observation is noted in the caption of Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In all experiments testing TPMPA effects, [Ca2+]o was 4 mM (presumably maximizing the confounding effects of postsynaptic factors) and the recording temperature was ~22°C.
source: In all experiments, [Ca2+]o was 4 mM (presumably maximizing the confounding effects of postsynaptic factors) and the recording temperature was ∼22°C.
evidence: This experimental condition is stated in the caption of Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The absolute value of the slope of the TCR-peak release rate relation is ~12 times higher for loose (200 nm) than for tight (20 nm) coupling in the fixed coupling distance model.
source: Note that the absolute value of the slope is ∼12 times and ∼7 times higher, respectively, for loose than for tight coupling.
evidence: This quantitative comparison is stated in the caption of Figure 3.

claim: The absolute value of the slope of the TCR-peak release rate relation is ~7 times higher for loose (200 nm) than for tight (20 nm) coupling in the variable coupling distance model.
source: Note that the absolute value of the slope is ∼12 times and ∼7 times higher, respectively, for loose than for tight coupling.
evidence: This quantitative comparison is stated in the caption of Figure 3.

claim: The absolute value of the slope of the TCR-peak release rate relation is higher for loose than for tight coupling in models with increased concentration of endogenous fixed buffer or reduced Ca2+-unbinding rate of the fixed buffer.
source: Note that the absolute value of the slope is higher for loose than for tight coupling in all cases.
evidence: This observation is stated in the caption of Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In all experiments with Ca2+ chelators, the presynaptic basket cell was patched twice to demonstrate recovery.
source: In all experiments included in (B) and (D), the presynaptic BC was patched twice to demonstrate recovery.
evidence: This experimental design detail is stated in the caption of Figure 4.

claim: Confidence intervals of coupling distance were obtained by bootstrap procedures using 1000 artificial data sets.
source: Confidence intervals of coupling distance were obtained by bootstrap procedures. 1000 artificial data sets were generated from the means and SEMs of the original data set and analyzed as the original (Efron and Tibshirani, 1998).
evidence: This statistical method is described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Error estimates for coupling distance were given as half of the 15.9–84.1 percentile range.
source: Error estimates were given as half of the 15.9–84.1 percentile range.
evidence: This statistical approach is described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: A previously published Hodgkin-Huxley-type gating model of P/Q-type Ca2+ channels was used to calculate the Ca2+ inflow.
source: A previously published Hodgkin-Huxley-type gating model of P/Q-type Ca2+ channels was used to calculate the Ca2+ inflow (Borst and Sakmann, 1998).
evidence: This modeling approach is described in the Materials and methods section with a supporting citation.

claim: Vesicular release rate was computed using a model of transmitter release originally established at the calyx of Held.
source: Vesicular release rate was computed using a model of transmitter release originally established at the calyx of Held (Lou et al., 2005).
evidence: This modeling approach is described in the Materials and methods section with a supporting citation.

claim: This model was preferred over alternative models because it is based on the most extensive set of experimental data.
source: This model was preferred over alternative models because it is based on the most extensive set of experimental data.
evidence: This justification for model choice is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: To account for the rapid timing of transmitter release at BC–PC synapses, the previously used presynaptic action potential was time-compressed by a factor of two, Ca2+ channel gating rates were multiplied by a factor of two, and the binding and unbinding rates of the sensor were increased by a factor of two.
source: To account for the rapid timing of transmitter release at BC–PC synapses, the previously used presynaptic action potential (Meinrenken et al., 2002; Bucurenciu et al., 2008) was time-compressed by a factor of two, Ca2+ channel gating rates were multiplied by a factor of two, and the binding and unbinding rates of the sensor were increased by a factor of two.
evidence: These model adjustments are described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: In simulations with distributed arrangement of release sensors, a coefficient of variation for the coupling distance of 0.3 was assumed.
source: In a subset of simulations, a distributed arrangement of release sensors was assumed, with a coefficient of variation for the coupling distance of 0.3 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This model parameter is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: For simulations with distributed sensors, release rates were obtained at various distances, and the average release rate was computed as the weighted mean, with weight factors set according to a normal distribution.
source: In these cases, release rates were obtained at various distances, and the average release rate was computed as the weighted mean, with weight factors set according to a normal distribution.
evidence: This computational approach is described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Experiments were performed in strict accordance with institutional, national, and European guidelines for animal experimentation.
source: Experiments were performed in strict accordance with institutional, national, and European guidelines for animal experimentation.

source: Mice were maintained under light (7 am–7 pm) and dark cycle (7 pm–7 am) conditions and were kept in a litter of 8 animals together with the mother in a single cage.
evidence: This animal husbandry detail is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Parasagittal 250-µm-thick cerebellar slices from the vermis region were cut using a custom-built vibratome.
source: Parasagittal 250-µm-thick cerebellar slices from the vermis region were cut using a custom-built vibratome.
evidence: This methodological detail is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: After ~20 min incubation at ~35°C, the slices were stored at room temperature.
source: After ∼20 min incubation at ∼35°C, the slices were stored at room temperature.
evidence: This methodological detail is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Experiments were performed at 21–23°C, unless specified differently, or at either 11–13°C or 32–35°C in subsets of experiments as indicated.
source: Experiments were performed at 21–23°C, unless specified differently, or at either 11–13°C or 32–35°C in subsets of experiments as indicated.
evidence: This experimental condition is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Presynaptic pipette resistance was 12–15 MΩ.
source: Presynaptic pipette resistance was 12–15 MΩ.
evidence: This methodological detail is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Postsynaptic pipette resistance was 0.8–1.5 MΩ, resulting in a mean series resistance of 3.8 ± 0.1 MΩ (range: 2.5–7.5 MΩ, 92 cells).
source: Postsynaptic pipette resistance was 0.8–1.5 MΩ, resulting in a mean series resistance of 3.8 ± 0.1 MΩ (range: 2.5–7.5 MΩ, 92 cells).
evidence: This methodological detail is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Postsynaptic series resistance was not compensated, but continuously monitored using 5-mV test pulses.
source: Postsynaptic series resistance was not compensated, but continuously monitored using 5-mV test pulses.
evidence: This methodological detail is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Experiments were only analyzed if changes in series resistance in the entire recording period were less than 2 MΩ.
source: Experiments were only analyzed if changes in series resistance in the entire recording period were less than 2 MΩ.
evidence: This quality control criterion is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Experiments were discarded if there was a detectable rundown of IPSC peak amplitude during the control period.
source: Similarly, experiments were discarded if there was a detectable rundown of IPSC peak amplitude during the control period.
evidence: This quality control criterion is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: For intracellular stimulation of BCs in the whole-cell configuration under current-clamp conditions, single pulses (400 pA, 4 ms at ~22°C and ~34°C; 500 pA, 5 ms at ~12°C) were injected into the BC every 4 s (~22°C and ~34°C) or 15 s (~12°C).
source: For intracellular stimulation of BCs in the whole-cell configuration under current-clamp conditions, single pulses (400 pA, 4 ms at ∼22°C and ∼34°C; 500 pA, 5 ms at ∼12°C) were injected into the BC every 4 s (∼22°C and ∼34°C) or 15 s (∼12°C).
evidence: This methodological detail is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: A holding current of ~ –50 pA was applied to maintain the resting membrane potential at ~–65 mV and to avoid spontaneous action potential generation.
source: A holding current of ∼ –50 pA was applied to maintain the resting membrane potential at ∼–65 mV and to avoid spontaneous action potential generation.
evidence: This methodological detail is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: For cell-attached stimulation under voltage-clamp conditions, action potentials were evoked by brief voltage pulses (amplitude <1 V, duration 0.1–0.2 ms).
source: For cell-attached stimulation under voltage-clamp conditions (Perkins, 2006; Vyleta and Jonas, 2014), the presynaptic pipette contained a K+-based intracellular solution. Action potentials were evoked by brief voltage pulses (amplitude <1 V, duration 0.1–0.2 ms).
evidence: This methodological detail is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Pipette holding potential for cell-attached stimulation was set to −60 or −80 mV to minimize the holding current and to avoid spontaneous action potential generation.
source: Pipette holding potential was set to −60 or −80 mV to minimize the holding current and to avoid spontaneous action potential generation.
evidence: This methodological detail is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Experiments in which presynaptic seal resistance went below 1 GΩ during recording were discarded.
source: Experiments in which presynaptic seal resistance went below 1 GΩ during recording were discarded.
evidence: This quality control criterion is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: In all experiments, PCs were recorded under voltage-clamp conditions at a holding potential of −70 mV.
source: In all experiments, PCs were recorded under voltage-clamp conditions at a holding potential of −70 mV.
evidence: This methodological detail is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Membrane potentials given were not corrected for liquid junction potentials.
source: Membrane potentials given were not corrected for liquid junction potentials.
evidence: This methodological note is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Bovine serum albumin was added at a concentration of 1 mg ml−1 to prevent adsorption of peptides to the surfaces of the perfusion system.
source: Bovine serum albumin (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MI) was added at a concentration of 1 mg ml−1 to prevent adsorption of peptides to the surfaces of the perfusion system.
evidence: This methodological detail is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Signals were filtered at 6 kHz (4-pole low-pass Bessel filter) and digitized at 20 or 50 kHz.
source: Signals were filtered at 6 kHz (4-pole low-pass Bessel filter) and digitized at 20 or 50 kHz using a CED 1401plus interface (Cambridge Electronic Design, UK).
evidence: This methodological detail is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Synaptic latency was determined as the time from the steepest point of the rise phase of the presynaptic action potential to the onset of the IPSC.
source: Synaptic latency (the steepest point of the rise phase of the presynaptic action potential to the onset of the IPSC), and proportion of failures were determined from 50 to 800 single traces.
evidence: This definition is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: For deconvolution analysis, the time course of release was filtered at 5 kHz (for recordings at ~22°C or ~34°C) or 0.5 kHz (for measurements at ~12°C) using a digital filter.
source: For subsequent analysis and display, the TCR was filtered at 5 kHz (for recordings at ∼22°C or ∼34°C) or 0.5 kHz (for measurements at ∼12°C) using a digital filter.
evidence: This methodological detail is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The effects of filtering on the time course of release were corrected by subtracting the variance of an impulse response of a Gaussian filter.
source: The effects of filtering were corrected by subtracting the variance of an impulse response of a Gaussian filter (Colquhoun and Sigworth, 1995).
evidence: This methodological detail is stated in the Materials and methods section with a supporting citation.

claim: Statistical significance was tested using a two-sided Wilcoxon signed rank test for paired data, a two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test for unpaired data, and a Kruskal–Wallis test for multiple comparisons.
source: Statistical significance was tested using a two-sided Wilcoxon signed rank test for paired data, a two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test for unpaired data, and a Kruskal–Wallis test for multiple comparisons (Igor Pro 6.3.2).
evidence: This statistical methodology is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Differences with p < 0.05 were considered significant.
source: Differences with p < 0.05 were considered significant.
evidence: This statistical criterion is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Ca2+ diffusion and binding to mobile and fixed buffers were modeled using the full set of partial differential equations (PDEs) of the reaction–diffusion problem.
source: Ca2+ diffusion and binding to mobile and fixed buffers were modeled using the full set of partial differential equations (PDEs) of the reaction–diffusion problem, including all necessary boundary and initial conditions (Smith, 2001; Bucurenciu et al., 2008; Eggermann and Jonas, 2012; Vyleta and Jonas, 2014).
evidence: This modeling approach is described in the Materials and methods section with supporting citations.

claim: PDEs were solved numerically with NDSolve of Mathematica 8.01 running under Windows 7 on a PC.
source: PDEs were solved numerically with NDSolve of Mathematica 8.01 running under Windows 7 on a PC.
evidence: This computational detail is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: PDEs were integrated over the radial coordinate (2000 grid points) and solved at a concentration accuracy of 0.01 nM.
source: PDEs were integrated over the radial coordinate (2000 grid points) and solved at a concentration accuracy of 0.01 nM.
evidence: This computational detail is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: For the fixed endogenous Ca2+ buffer, the rates were chosen as kon = 5 × 10^8 M^−1 s^−1 and koff = 1000 s^−1 (affinity 2 µM).
source: For the fixed endogenous Ca2+ buffer, the rates were chosen as kon = 5 108 M−1 s−1 and koff = 1000 s−1 (affinity 2 µM).
evidence: This model parameter is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: For standard simulations, both a fixed buffer (100 µM) and a mobile buffer with BAPTA-like properties (10 µM) were incorporated.
source: For standard simulations, both a fixed buffer (100 µM) and a mobile buffer with BAPTA-like properties (10 µM) were incorporated.
evidence: This model parameter is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Ca2+ buffer concentrations were considered to be spatially uniform.
source: Ca2+ buffer concentrations were considered to be spatially uniform.
evidence: This model assumption is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The occupancies for the different states of the release sensor model were obtained by solving the corresponding first-order ordinary differential equations with a Q-matrix approach.
source: The occupancies for the different states of the model were obtained by solving the corresponding first-order ordinary differential equations with a Q-matrix approach.
evidence: This computational approach is described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Release rate was computed as the sum of the product of occupancy and release rate for each state; pool depletion was not considered.
source: Release rate was computed as the sum of the product of occupancy and release rate for each state; pool depletion was not considered.
evidence: This computational approach is described in the Materials and methods section.
